extracted.intended_audience: legislators, statesmen, and educated readers interested in constitutional design, military governance, and public finance
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the structure and conduct of a revolutionary government's constitution, military arrangements, municipal powers, and public finance. The page offers practical political judgements about how institutional arrangements affect order, obedience, and state capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of military and municipal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipalities must not arrogate authority over the troops; the institutions have reserved military authority wholly to the monarch and fixed limits of municipal action to requisition. The letter or spirit of decrees do not authorize commons to break officers, try them, give orders to soldiers, drive them from posts, stop marches ordered by the king, or enslave troops to the caprice of cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "You have fixed the limits of the military authority and the municipal authority... never did the letter or the spirit of your decrees authorise the commons in these municipalities to break the officers, to try them, to give orders to the soldiers, to drive them from the posts committed to their guard, to stop them in their marches ordered by the king, or, in a word, to enslave the troops to the caprice of each of the cities..." — use this as a standard for judging whether municipal powers improperly intrude on military command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mingling soldiers with municipal societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Encouraging free conversation, feasts, and civic confederacies between soldiers and municipal festive societies will likely undermine military discipline and draw soldiers into the habits and sympathies of the lowest and most desperate parts of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that mixing soldiers in municipal clubs and confederacies will create elective attractions drawing them away from officers: "If the soldiers once come to mix for any time in the municipal clubs, cabals, and confederacies, an elective attraction will draw them to the lowest and most desperate part." Avoid policies that normalize civic fraternization that replaces military subordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal, vigorous authority as basis of military obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Military obedience requires a real, vigorous, effective, decided, personal authority (traditionally the sovereign) rather than a transient or collective assembly whose orders pass through debilitating channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "They must be constrained ... by a real, vigorous, effective, decided, personal authority." Evaluate whether the nominal head of the army is a cipher or commands genuine gratitude/fear; an assembly with short duration cannot reliably produce military obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of officer appointment and promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The way officers are nominated and promoted (court appointment, assembly approbation, election, seniority) shapes faction, discipline, and the character of the officer corps. Double negotiation (court plus assembly) or electioneering corrupts promotion and promotes faction; seniority-only produces formality and a 'military republic'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid systems where officers must canvass in the Assembly or depend on factional interests. Beware that allowing assemblies to have effective vetoes or enabling soldiers to exercise negatives on choice leads to political intrigues and divides the corps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the chain of military subordination against civic egalitarian doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching soldiers that they are 'citizens' with the rights of men, including the notion they should choose or reject officers, undermines the central link of obedience between officer and soldier and leads to mutinous tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The soldier is told, he is a citizen, and has the rights of man... He will therefore... exercise at least a negative in the choice of his officers." Evaluate doctrines or laws for their likely effect on obedience and the officer-soldier relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on military coercion as primary instrument of rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Where institutions have destroyed opinions and instincts that support government, the state is left to rule by an army; but principles taught to that army can make it unusable for the purposes the rulers intend, producing contradiction and eventual failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Every thing depends upon the army in such a government as yours; for you have industriously destroyed all the opinions, and prejudices... Therefore the moment any difference arises... you must have recourse to force." Use this to judge the sustainability and legitimacy of coercive enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of municipal (militia) armies unconnected to central authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A municipal army formed, armed, and officered at district pleasure, unconnected to the crown or national institutions, is democratic and uniform in itself but becomes a 'monster' when related to the crown, assembly, tribunals, or other army — likely to cause national calamity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "If considered in any relation to the crown... it seems a monster, and can hardly fail to terminate its perplexed movements in some great national calamity." Judge local militia schemes by their coherence with national institutions and potential to generate conflict of loyalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional coherence and reciprocal relations of institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The weaknesses or imbecilities of one constitutional part (crown, assembly, military, judicature) will expose and aggravate the insufficiency and mischief of other parts; remedies must consider the whole reciprocal relation, not isolated fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The imbecility of any part... cannot be laid open without discovering the utter insufficiency and mischief of every other part with which it comes in contact." Use systemic analysis: reforms must avoid creating contradictory or competing authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between rhetorical rights and practical redress
rubrics_metrics.description: Public leaders who loudly teach metaphysical 'rights' but fail to provide practical redress or to abolish grievous effects (e.g., feudal rents) provoke resentment; preaching rights without remedy undermines legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether declarations of rights are matched by policies that actually relieve grievances. The text criticizes leaders who 'tell them of their rights... and they tell them afterwards how much of that barbarous tyranny they are to bear with patience.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy and enforceability of taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxation requires a perceived lawful authority to exact payment; if people judge the assembly to lack legitimate authority, they may refuse to pay taxes, forcing recourse to troops which undermines consent and stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Why should they not? What lawful authority is there left to exact them? ... To this the answer is, We will send troops." Assess tax measures not only on policy but on whether the enforcing authority is seen as legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial-administration competence and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: A financier's duties: secure an ample revenue; impose it with judgment and equality; employ it economically; use credit when necessary; found finances on clearness and candour of proceedings, exactness of calculations, and solidity of funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The objects of a financier are, then, to secure an ample revenue; to impose it with judgment and equality; to employ it economically; and, when necessity obliges him, to make use of credit. ... by the clearness and candour of his proceedings, the exactness of his calculations, and the solidity of his funds." Use these as performance criteria when judging fiscal policy and ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate and balanced public revenue as foundation of state capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Revenue is the spring of all power; public virtue and the capacity to undertake great public functions depend on having an ample, properly balanced revenue — between what supports individuals and what is collected for common efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The revenue of the State is the state... Through the revenue alone the body politic can act in its true genius and character." Evaluate reforms by their effect on the adequacy and balance of revenue, and by whether they preserve the state's ability to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts of interest in property and reform by legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators who have acquired landed property by confiscation (or otherwise) have incentives to preserve market values and rents, producing inconsistency: they may abrogate honours but preserve rents to protect their own new property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author points out self-interested behaviour: "They had newly possessed themselves of a great body of landed property by confiscation... The only security which property enjoys... is from the interests of their rapacity with regard to some other." Use conflict-of-interest analysis when judging property reforms.
